newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China to check HK political reform--Briton adviser.
newsitem.headline: China to check HK political reform--Briton adviser.

text.p: China will give Hong Kong great economic autonomy but never allow political reform, a leading architect of the colony's laissez-faire economy said on Friday.

Briton Jimmy McGregor, a pillar of Hong Kong for decades and close adviser to outgoing governor Chris Patten, forecast a bleak future for democratic activists under Beijing's rule and said people would think twice about demonstrating in the streets.

"The Chinese authorities have no intention of letting Hong Kong develop as a political embarrassment," said McGregor, leaving politics as Britain hands Hong Kong back to China after 156 years of colonial rule.
He said of forthcoming Chinese rule:"The overall policy is to restrain the political development of Hong Kong."
McGregor has bowed to the wishes of his Hong Kong Chinese wife who wants them to go and live in Canada,
Patten was vilified by Beijing for instituting democratic reforms and seeking to protect human rights in the runup to the June 30 handover.
Democrat Martin Lee, who says Patten's successor Tung Chee-hwa is a Beijing puppet, became the most popular politician in Hong Kong with his election victories in the legislature.
McGregor said of the democrats under China: "I think they are going to be restricted in some way or another."
Tens of thousands of Hong Kong Chinese took to the streets this month to mark the latest anniversary of the 1989 crushing of China's Tiananmen democracy protest. McGregor doubted a repeat.
"One hundred different things can be done to discourage people taking to the streets," he told a lunch honouring him at the Foreign Correspondents' Club.
"Many will have to decide in their own minds -- is it worth risking my job?" he added,

The 73-year-old McGregor, target of communist death threats in the Cultural Revolution 30 years ago was much more optimistic about the chances of Hong Kong's booming economy thriving without interference.
"China wants this place to continue to be successful, to produce the golden eggs," he said.

McGregor, whose departure marks the end of an era after 50 years at the centre of Hong Kong life, predicted that the dizzying pace of economic change in communist China would inevitably provoke political change.
"The system they have now ... cannot exist alongside a market economy," said the Scot, who leaves with a heavy heart and confessed to reporters "I lost the argument with my wife."
